title: The spookiest haunted places in London: 7 of the city's eeriest hideouts
excerpt: London's eeriest spots, from ancient fortresses haunted by captive royals to historic pubs where things go bump in the night
content:
I’ve always had a fascination with the supernatural, perhaps because my birthday is Halloween and it’s been a significant day for me all my life. Or it could be due to the fact I’ve had my own ghost sighting, when I was living in my university accommodation in Manchester many years ago. The ghostly little girl who lived in my room is definitely the spookiest thing to have happened to me and it’s a story I still tell people at parties. Some people believe me, some don’t. It was an eerie, terrifying and curious experience and one that’s meant I’m a little obsessed with haunted places and the legendary lore behind them.

Luckily, London is packed with paranormal activity, ghostly movements and spiritual awakenings, so I can get my spooky fix year-round. Below, I've rounded up some of my favourites for you to visit this Halloween season.

7 most haunted places in London

The Tower of London

When it comes to haunted spots in the city, The Tower of London can’t be missed. Not only is it a site of major historical significance, but it’s here that you’ll find the spirits of many royals, including the ghosts of Henry VIII’s former wife Anne Boleyn, a murdered king, and the ‘Nine Days Queen’ Lady Jane Grey. Oh, and a ghostly bear.

Address: Tower of London, London EC3N 4AB
Website: hrp.org.uk

Hampton Court Palace

If you’re looking for a potential sighting of more ghostly royals, Hampton Court Palace is next on your haunted list. And yes, it’s Henry VIII’s wives once again. These women remain steadfast in their impact. Jane Seymour died at Hampton Court, only a few days after delivering Henry’s son, Prince Edward. A pale figure is reported to appear on the Silverstick Stairs, which once led up to a room in which Jane gave birth, and died.

The ghost of Catherine Howard, Henry VIII's fifth queen, is a little more vocal. In fact, she’s a screamer. Catherine was beheaded at the Tower of London in 1542, for adultery and treason. It’s claimed that after she was arrested at Hampton Court, she broke free of her guards and ran along what is now called the Haunted Gallery, screaming out to the king for mercy. She never reached him, but it’s said that her ghost now repeats this tragic journey.

Address: Hampton Court Palace, Hampton Ct Way, Molesey, East Molesey KT8 9AU
Website: hrp.org.uk

St James’ Park

In 1804, soldiers of the Coldstream Guards reported strange experiences while they were on duty in St. James’s Park, with one officer even submitting a signed declaration of what he’d seen. According to the soldiers, they saw a headless woman in a red dress appear around the lake and Birdcage Walk. And there have been more recent sightings of this ghost, including in the early 1970s.

The backstory (which historians haven’t been able to find evidence for) of this mystery woman is that an army sergeant beheaded his wife in the park and attempted to dispose of her body in the lake. This woman became known as the ‘headless lady’ or ‘red lady’ of the park, where she rises from the water and runs across the park, looking for her lost head.

Address: St James' Park, London SW1A 2BJ
Website: royalparks.org.uk

The Ten Bells

Jack the Ripper’s famed local pub, The Ten Bells, is quite the flurry of paranormal activity. In 1996, the landlord claimed The Ten Bells had been taken over by the ghost of Annie Chapman, murdered by the Ripper in 1888. And there have been multiple reports of something spooky going on here, with customers and bar staff reporting hearing footsteps in empty corridors and experiencing unexplained cold spots in the pub.

Address: The Ten Bells, 84 Commercial Street, London E1 6LY
Website: tenbells.com

Bank Station

On the London Underground, Bank Station has one of the most famous and long-lasting ghost stories on the network: the spirit of Sarah Whitehead, nicknamed the ‘Black Nun’. According to legend, her brother Philip Whitehead worked for the Bank of England in the 1800s and he was arrested for forgery, then executed. Sarah was devastated and apparently began going to the Bank of England and asking to see her brother, dressed in black mourning clothes… And these visits may or may not have continued after her death.

Address: Bank Station, Underground Ltd, Bank/Monument Complex, Princes St, London EC3V 3LA
Website: tfl.gov.uk

The Gatehouse, Highgate

This pub in Highgate isn’t just haunted by one ghost, oh no. There are a few who have taken up residency here. The most famous spirit is that of Mother Marnes, supposedly a Jacobean woman murdered for her wealth, who likes to roam around the upstairs of the building.

There have also been several accounts describing a tall figure in old-fashioned clothing, who also likes to haunt the upstairs of The Gatehouse. Then in 1966, a man named Tony Abbott was at the pub and reportedly saw a tall figure wearing a hat moving along a corridor and entering the room. According to Abbott’s account, the light went out, the room went cold, and he experienced a rushing sound followed by the sensation that something was strangling him.

Address: The Gatehouse, 1 North Road, Highgate Village, London N6 4BD
Website: urbanpubsandbars.com

Queen's House, Greenwich (the Tulip Staircase)

There are myths and legends; then there’s photographic evidence. In the case of the Tulip Staircase, the Queen’s House ghost seemed to have been captured in an image.

In 1966, a retired Canadian reverend and his wife visited the Queen’s House. The Reverend and Mrs R. W. Hardy had heard about the famous Tulip Stairs and took a photograph. It wasn’t until they developed it once they were back home, that they saw it had also captured the image of a shrouded figure. On closer inspection, the figure appears to be ascending the stairs in pursuit of a second figure, and possibly a third.

The couple were adamant that the stairs were clear when they took the photo, and a thorough investigation shortly after it was taken couldn’t provide a definitive, rational explanation for what the picture shows. And so, the mystery continues.

Address: Queen's House, Romney Road, London SE10 9NF
Website: rmg.co.uk
